qAndA.answer: The scientist shows a bottle of Malachite Green which is a dark color, the label states 'Malachite Green', however it looks more blue than green.
qAndA.question: What color is Malachite Green?

qAndA.answer: Heating the slide helps to drive the Malachite Green stain into the tough outer layers of the endospores.
qAndA.question: Why is it important to heat the slide over a water bath during the staining process?

qAndA.answer: The endospores appear green after staining with Malachite Green.
qAndA.question: What color are the endospores after the staining procedure?

qAndA.answer: The vegetative bacterial cells are stained pink by the counterstain Safranin.
qAndA.question: What color are the vegetative bacterial cells after the staining procedure?

qAndA.answer: Control smears with known endospore-producing and non-endospore-producing bacteria help to validate the effectiveness of the staining procedure and to ensure accurate identification of endospores in the unknown sample.
qAndA.question: What is the purpose of using control smears in the endospore staining procedure?

narrativeProgression.description: The scientist introduces her prepared endospore slide and points out the locations of her unknown sample and controls.
She applies Malachite Green, the primary stain, to the slide, making sure all areas are covered.
The slide is placed on a water bath for 3-5 minutes to allow the heat to drive the stain into the endospores.
After the allotted time, the slide is removed, and excess stain is allowed to drip off.
The slide is rinsed with water to remove excess Malachite Green.
Safranin, the counterstain, is applied to the slide to stain the vegetative bacterial cells.
The slide is rinsed again with water to remove excess Safranin.
The scientist gently blots the slide dry with a paper towel, avoiding rubbing to prevent damaging the bacterial smears.
The scientist shows the finished slide with all three smears ready for observation.
A new scene begins with an image of another finished slide.

narrativeProgression.description: Another finished slide is shown, with its control smears and the unknown smear. Bacillus subtilis and Staphylococcus epidermidis are used as positive and negative controls, respectively.
A microscopic view of the Bacillus subtilis smear is presented, showcasing the green endospores and the pink vegetative cells.
A microscopic view of the Staphylococcus epidermidis smear is shown, displaying only pink vegetative cells, confirming its non-endospore-producing nature.
The video concludes by promoting the website ScienceProfOnline.com for more free science education resources.

timecoded_text_to_speech.text: In this video I'm going to show you how to do an endospor stain.
Hello!
First we need to put on our eye protection.
Here's our endospor staining procedure.
The first step is to apply the primary stain Malachite Green.
This is done over a water bath for 3 to 5 minutes.
The heat from the water bath will drive that green stain into the endospor.
Next we'll rinse the slide with water and the final stop is to apply the counter stain.
Saferin.
This pink stain is a contrasting color to the green and the limparate color to the vegetative bacterial cells.
We begin by applying the primary stain in a fume hood.
Here's my prepared endospor slide.
My unknown is in the center circle and my two controls are in the outer circles.
I place my slide over the water bath and now I'm ready to apply the primary stain Malachite Green.
I drip the Malachite Green directly onto my slide, making sure that each of those circles are completely covered with stain.
Allow the stained slide to heat over the water bath for 3 to 5 minutes.
It's important not to let that stain dry out so if it looks like it's beginning to dry out, you can apply more Malachite Green.
After 3 to 5 minutes, I retrieve my slide, allowing any excess stain to drip off into the water bath.
I then place the slide on a paper towel and take it back to my station to finish the stained procedure.
The next step is to rinse the Malachite Green off the slide.
After rinsing, I'm now ready to apply my counter stain, saffonin.
The Malachite Green was easier to use than the original one.
After rinsing, I'm now ready to apply my counter stain, saffonin.
The Malachite Green was used to stain the endospores.
The counter stain saffonin is used to stain the bacterial cells, a contrasting color.
Once I've applied the saffonin to cover all 3 circles, all 3 bacterial smears, I wait 1 minute.
Now it's time to rinse the saffonin off of my slide.
After rinsing, I'm going to gently blot that slide dry.
Don't rub the slide or you can wipe off the bacterial smears, just gently blot.
Here's my finished slide.
Here's another example of an endospore stained slide.
I have my unknown smear in the center.
To the left is my positive control, my known endospore producer.
In the sample I use Bicillus subtilus.
Here it is under the scope, under oil and immersion, magnified 1,000 times.
The little green ovals are the endospores and the pink rods are the vegetative cells.
The bacterial smear on the right is my nonendospore producer, which would be my negative control.
In this case, I use Staphylococcus.
Here's what my negative control looks like under the scope.
This is Staphylococcus epidermidis.
It does not produce endospores, so I see only pink vegetative cells.

youtube_description:
Step-by-step video and audio instructions on how to endospore stain a slide that includes three bacterial smears; an endospore + control (known endospore producing bacteria), an endospore - control (known non-endospore producing bacteria) and an unknown.

For a video on how to prepare a bacterial smear slide for endospore staining see:     http://youtu.be/M-EMFGtpIpI

Video by Tami (Guy) Port, Chief Executive Nerd at ScienceProfOnline.com. For the lab materials that go with this movie, see the Virtual Microbiology Classroom Identification of Unknown Bacteria Laboratory Main Page at ScienceProfOnline.com.
